# RV power station and solar combos

The best combo depends on whether you run air conditioning and how long you stay off-grid. I couldn't pull direct retailer listings, so the links go to the review pages with the current-price buttons. Those pages are affiliate sites, and their specs and prices differ in places, so confirm on the retailer's page before buying.

## Weekend trips, fridge, devices, Starlink
**Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 + two SolarSaga 200W panels**
- It has 1,070Wh, 1,500W output, a 400W solar input limit and weighs about 24 lb. Two 200W panels use the full input, so extra panels won't charge it faster. It isn't expandable. ([Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))
- The older Explorer 1000 Plus (1,264Wh) is also recommended for light use. ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife))

## Best overall for camping and part-time RVing
**EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus + EcoFlow folding or rigid panels**
- It has 1,024Wh, 1,800W output, and two 500W solar inputs (1,000W total) for a roughly 70-minute full-sun recharge. It expands to 5kWh and recharges from a wall outlet in about 56 minutes.
- To use that solar ceiling you need two separate panel connections. A single 200W panel works but charges slower. ([Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))

## Multi-day boondocking, mid-size budget
**Bluetti AC200L + a large panel array**
- It has 2,048Wh, 2,400W output, up to 1,200W solar input and a built-in 30A RV port. It weighs about 62 lb. ([Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/), [EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- For panels, NomadSignal suggests the Renogy 200W Foldable Solar Suitcase. ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife))

## Full-time RV living or running the roof AC
- **EcoFlow Delta Pro 3:** 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous, 8,000W surge, expandable past 12kWh. It is heavy, a two-person lift, and the most expensive option. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro:** 3,024Wh and 3,000W, enough to start a 13,500 BTU AC without a soft-start kit. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes above 3,000W at startup, so a 1,000W-class unit won't work for it.

## Buying tips
- **Match panels to the solar input limit.** A big array on a low-input unit is wasted. Bluetti's older AC200P, for example, caps at 700W. ([Outdoor Power Stations](https://outdoorpowerstations.com/articles/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti))
- **Size by load.** Multiply watts by hours. A 150W fridge for 10 hours is about 1,500Wh. ([Acquired Sense](https://www.acquiredsense.com/reviews/power-stations.html))
- **Choose LiFePO4.** All the models above use it, and it is rated for thousands of cycles.
- **Skip the safety section in the EmergencyEnergy article.** Its rules are for Ontario, Canada, not the US. Hire a licensed electrician for any hardwired RV connection.

If you tell me your RV type, whether you have roof AC, and how many nights you go without hookups, I can narrow this to one pick and a specific panel size.
